parsed.explanation: A trans woman presenting female is directly criminalised by Section 379, with up to three months' imprisonment for appearance alone. The same-sex statute was reported unenforced 2018-2022, but security forces were reported to harass, arrest, detain, torture and beat LGBTQI+ people in that period, a minister threatened detention until procreation, a support group was raided and closed, and most openly LGBTQI+ citizens fled hostile state action. No hate-crime or broad anti-discrimination protection, no support organisations, and no documented remedy exist. Entry, facility and care rules are undocumented, not safe; structural signals extrapolate to severe state-perpetrated risk if outed.

entry_documents.exposure: Section 379 criminalises male presentation as female in public, so document/presentation mismatch at any check can trigger arrest; specific entry screening of trans visitors is not documented.
entry_documents.interaction: Border, police or hotel document check could convert mismatch into investigation under Section 379.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Security forces reported to harass, arrest, detain, torture and beat LGBTQI+ persons, 2018-2022; a community group was raided in 2017 and staff detained for months without charge.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Arrest for presentation could lead to detention and abusive custody with no documented oversight or consular remedy.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Section 379 dress offence; unnatural-offence statute up to 10 years remains on books though reported unenforced; 2017 minister ordered arrest/detention until procreation; hostile official rhetoric; NGO Act constrains support groups.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Only oil/gas employee harassment prohibition as of 2020; not a visitor protection.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Law plus documented security-force abuse creates state threat-framing, not merely social disapproval.

minors_guardians.exposure: No age-specific rule documented; a travelling minor faces same presentation, detention and lack-of-recourse environment through a guardian who could also be detained or separated.
minors_guardians.interaction: Guardian detention could leave a minor without care; family-based exposure is not documented.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Widespread societal stigma; security forces themselves are documented perpetrators of harassment and beatings, and most openly LGBTQI+ citizens fled due to hostile government action.
street_violence_police_response.protection: No hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection documented.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Police are exposure source rather than protection; victims have no documented organisation to report to.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No LGBTQ-support organisations; support group raided, closed and director left; enforcement of Section 379 itself and formalisation of 2017 detention statement are not sourced.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Absence of organisations and legal protection means documented abuses have no recorded remedy.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar: presentation criminalised, detainees beaten, courts/recourse illusory. This case lacks a capital provision and documented routine Section 379 prosecutions, but documented torture by security forces keeps it near this anchor rather than safer.

Lower than this anchor: 0.25 has raids, fines, extortion and rare imprisonment with some court overturns. Here security forces tortured and beat people, a group was closed after months' detention, and the community largely fled, indicating worse state-perpetrated severity and thinner recourse.

Much lower: 0.35 involves stops, confiscation, fines and ineffective complaints but detention rarely becomes imprisonment and lethal force is not threatened. Documented torture, beatings and a direct dress offence place this case well below 0.35.

parsed.synthesis: Combined regime is unitary and hostile: Section 379 makes public presentation itself an offence, while documented security-force harassment, detention, torture and beatings supply the enforcement reality behind the paper law. The unenforced same-sex statute does not mitigate this, because targeting is documented through security practice and official threats. With no hate-crime protection, no support organisations, a closed community group and mass flight by openly LGBTQI+ citizens, there is no operative recourse. Undocumented entry, facilities and care cannot be treated as safe; the documented exposure governs.
